title: Household and Metric Conversions

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a gram as a big pizza cut into 1,000 tiny slices. Each little slice is a milligram, so it takes 1,000 of those slices to rebuild the whole pizza. The prefix 'milli' is just a fancy way of saying 'one of a thousand pieces.'

### Question 2

A teaspoon is the little spoon you stir tea or cocoa with, and it holds about 5 mL of liquid. Remember 'small spoon, small number 5.' The bigger tablespoon and the ounce hold more, so they get bigger numbers.

### Question 3

The metric system has three main 'rulers': the meter measures how long, the gram measures how heavy, and the liter measures how much liquid fits inside. When you pour medicine, you are measuring liquid, so the liter is your ruler, and it splits into 1,000 mL.

### Question 4

A tablespoon (15 mL) is like three teaspoons (5 mL each) poured into one bigger spoon. If you only used one teaspoon when the label said tablespoon, you would give just a third of the medicine. Three teaspoons make one tablespoon, every time.

### Question 5

A kilogram is a little heavier than two pounds, so we use 2.2 as the conversion number. If you know someone's weight in pounds and want kilograms, you share it into groups of 2.2. It is like knowing that one big scoop equals two-and-a-bit little scoops.

### Question 6

One fluid ounce is just about 30 mL, really a touch under at 29.6, so nurses round it off to a clean 30, the way you would call a 29-minute show 'half an hour.' The dosing cup is marked with that rounded 30, and for everyday medicine amounts that tiny bit of rounding does not matter.

### Question 7

An inch is a bit longer than the width of your thumb, and it lines up with 2.54 of the tiny centimeter marks on a metric ruler. Centimeters are smaller, so it takes a couple-and-a-half of them to equal one inch. That same inch is 25.4 of the even tinier millimeter marks, and a meter is a big grown-up step, so no way could one inch be 25.4 meters. The number 2.54 is exact, not a guess.

### Question 8

Each liter is a bottle that fills 1,000 little mL cups. If you have two and a half of those big bottles, you count 1,000 plus 1,000 plus 500, which is 2,500 cups. Going to a smaller unit always makes the number bigger.

### Question 9

Grams are the big containers and milligrams are the tiny pieces, so it takes 1,000 mg to fill one gram. With only 750 mg you do not even have a full gram, you have 0.75 of one. The little zero in front of the dot is a safety flag that shouts 'less than one whole.'

### Question 10

A cup is 8 ounces stacked together, and each ounce is 30 mL. So you add 30 eight times, which lands on 240 mL. It is like knowing 8 candy bags with 30 candies each gives you 240 candies total.

### Question 11

Kilograms are heavier scoops than pounds, so it takes fewer of them to hold the same weight. Sharing 44 pounds into groups of 2.2 gives 20 kilograms. Going to the heavier unit makes the number shrink, not grow.

### Question 12

First turn each drink into mL: two cups make 480 mL, and four ounces make 120 mL. Then add the piles together, 480 plus 120, to get 600 mL. It is like counting coins from two jars separately, then pouring them into one total.
